parts.label: a
parts.technique: unbiased estimates of mean and variance from summary statistics
parts.reason: S2.3 covers standard deviation/variance from summary statistics (Sxx formula); unbiased variance estimate is a standard extension of this calculation.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: confidence interval for mean, known variance
parts.reason: No statement in S1-S5 covers confidence intervals; this concept (and z-interval for a mean) is not mentioned anywhere in the statements, so it is out of spec.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: probability using confidence interval result and normal distribution
parts.reason: This part depends directly on the answer to part (b) which is out of spec (confidence interval), and confidence intervals are not covered by any statement.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: hypothesis test for difference of two means using CLT/sampling distribution of sample mean
parts.reason: This requires the sampling distribution of the sample mean (CLT) for two samples, which is not covered by S5.3 (only tests for mean of a single Normal distribution) and explicitly S5.3 excludes CLT knowledge; two-sample tests are not mentioned anywhere.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: significance of Central Limit Theorem
parts.reason: S5.3 explicitly excludes 'Knowledge of the Central Limit Theorem or other large sample approximations is not required', so any question on CLT significance is out.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: calculate PMCC value
parts.reason: S5.1 explicitly states 'calculation of correlation coefficients is excluded' and S5.1 also states students calculate r using calculator, formula not required — but this part requires calculating r from Sxy, Sxx, Syy using the formula, which is the excluded calculation method.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: hypothesis test using PMCC compared to critical value
parts.reason: S5.1 explicitly covers extending hypothesis testing language to correlation coefficients, comparing a calculated r to a critical value/p-value, with hypotheses stated in terms of population correlation coefficient rho with null rho=0 — this is exactly what is described and is in spec (the exclusion is only on deriving/calculating r via formula, not on using an already-obtained r value in a test).

parts.label: c
parts.technique: assumption for PMCC hypothesis test (bivariate normality)
parts.reason: This is part of the standard hypothesis test procedure for correlation coefficient under S5.1, which requires an assumption about the underlying distribution being stated - a natural extension of the S5.1 test content.

parts.label: d
parts.technique: calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
parts.reason: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient is not mentioned anywhere in the statements; only PMCC (product moment correlation coefficient) is referenced in S5.1, and no rank correlation method is included.

parts.label: e
parts.technique: hypothesis test using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient
parts.reason: Depends on part (d)'s Spearman's coefficient, which is not covered by any statement (only PMCC is named); Spearman's is out of spec.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: quota sampling description
parts.reason: S1.1 explicitly lists quota sampling as a technique students should be familiar with, including describing how a sample could be obtained.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: chi-squared test for independence (contingency table)
parts.reason: Chi-squared tests, contingency tables, and tests of independence are not mentioned in any S1-S5 statement (only tests for binomial proportion, normal mean, and correlation coefficient are covered in S5), so this is out of spec.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: effect of scaling on chi-squared test statistic/critical value/conclusion
parts.reason: This depends entirely on the chi-squared test in part (b), which is out of spec, and chi-squared testing itself is not mentioned in any statement.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: sum of independent normal random variables, probability calculation
parts.reason: S4.2 covers the Normal distribution as a model and finding probabilities; combining independent normal variables (sum having a normal distribution) is a natural application of S3.1 (independence) and S4.2, though the specific 'sum of normals' result isn't explicitly named — this is a standard extension of S4.2/S3.1 content.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: difference of independent normal random variables, probability calculation
parts.reason: Similarly requires combining independent normal distributions (difference), extending S4.2's normal probability calculations and S3.1's independence — not explicitly stated as excluded, treated as an application of named content.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: inverse normal calculation for sum of normals
parts.reason: Uses the same combined normal distribution from part (a); finding t from a probability is a standard S4.2 percentile-type calculation on a normal distribution.

parts.label: d
parts.technique: binomial distribution probability using part (a) answer
parts.reason: S4.1 covers calculating binomial probabilities; this uses the probability from part (a) (itself judged in spec) as parameter p in a binomial model, so is a straightforward binomial calculation.

parts.label: e
parts.technique: critique of independence assumption in modelling
parts.reason: S4.3/S3.3 cover critiquing modelling assumptions including independence assumptions in probability models.

parts.label: a
parts.technique: normal probability calculation for expected frequencies
parts.reason: S4.2 covers finding probabilities using the Normal distribution, directly applicable to computing these expected frequency tail probabilities.

parts.label: b
parts.technique: chi-squared goodness-of-fit test
parts.reason: Chi-squared goodness-of-fit testing is not mentioned anywhere in the statements; only binomial proportion tests, normal mean tests, and correlation coefficient tests are listed in S5, so this is out of spec.

parts.label: c
parts.technique: effect of estimated parameters on chi-squared critical value (degrees of freedom)
parts.reason: This depends entirely on the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test framework from part (b), which is not covered by any statement.
